Longitudinal Analysis of Minimum Income Benefits in a French Local Authority

the {ViCaTraj} workflow

Elie Chosson

Table of contents

  • INTRODUCTION
  • 1. The data and the challenge
  • 2. The {ViCaTraj} workflow: database management and data formatting

  • Conclusion

INTRODUCTION

My role and work at the local authority

  • I work for the “Conseil départemental de l’Isère” (CD38), a French local authority governed by an elected council and president (population of 1.3 million, annual budget of €1.7 billion).

  • French “Departments” cover a wide range of areas, from roads and the environment to culture, but their core responsibilities are social services, including:

      1. child protection,
      1. support for older people and people with disabilities
      1. the “Revenu de Solidarité Active” (RSA): a benefit that guarantees a minimum income to households whose members are unemployed or have low earnings.
    • I work with longitudinal data across these 3 social areas, but today I’ll focus on how people’s perceptions of the RSA change over time.

  • Our two-person team evaluates the impact of the Department’s policies on residents using quantitative and qualitative methods.

Why conduct a longitudinal analysis at the Isère Departement?

  • Longitudinal analysis is increasingly common in the social sector because:

    • New data sources

    • New approaches to designing support and assistance programs, with a focus on activation, prevention (so on people’s pathways).

    • The growing use of policy experiments


  • For CD38, there is multiple interest to having this database updated and ready to use:

    • better understand the beneficiaries (seniority, ressources, …)

    • gaining a better understanding of the flows :

      • better understand the variations in volume
      • overcome the pessimistic outlook resulting from “stock” analysis and social workers’ feedback (as they rarely interact with individuals who quickly transition through the RSA)
      • see exits and returns (time, frequency)

    • contribute to the evaluation of pilot support programs for RSA recipients.

I contributed to this work during my PhD in economics, which I completed in 2017, then as a contractor for the Isère Departmental Council, and finally as an employee of the Department since 2023.

  • New data sources are becoming available, and public-sector professionals are developing the skills needed to manage and analyse them.

  • This trend also reflects a shift in how social policies are conceived. Increasingly, policies aim not only to provides support, but also to activate beneficiaries: to help them move forward in their pathways, gain autonomy, leave the benefit system, return to work. This raises questions that snapshot statistics cannot answer on their own: how do beneficiaries’ situations evolve over time, and how do social programs shape those trajectories?

  • This is happening alongside a rise in what are described as “experiments”: initiatives to test and refine support approaches and new social programs. But experimentation is also becoming a permanent mode of social-policy management, with repeated changes presented as temporary trials—potentially creating instability and allowing institutions to avoid making long-term commitments.

1. The data and the challenge

Data source

  • Raw household data on RSA are sent monthly by the “Caisse d’Allocation Familiale” to the CD38, in XML format

  • Each month the new xml delivery is reformatted into a tabular format and added to the parquet database, with:

    • one row per household
    • one column per variable (and per person, where needed)

  • In the workflow, other data can be linked on time and ID keys, if needed :

    • participation in support programmes

    • database of appointments with social workers

    • …

  • Raw dimensions of the final database :

    • each month, 117 variables stored to describe households and individuals: ➡️ age, family composition, dependent children, declared income, place of residence, homeless status, …

    • 4.123 million rows for the last 6 years, representing almost 74 000 housedolds and 87 000 individuals (childrens excluded) for last 72 months.

::: {.cell}

:::

Time steps and rows management

  • I analyse individual sequences of states.

  • I generally work with data in long format, with one varariable for time steps, one variable for ID, etc. and finally one row per observation.

    • In the longitudinal RSA data, time is genuinely discrete.
    • Sometimes, however, I need to work with continuous-time variables. In such cases, I discretise time.

  • This data structure is clear and efficient for processing, but :

    • With one row per individual per month, the previous or next row may not correspond to the adjacent calendar month.
      So missing data may appear as a missing row or an NA value.

    • Another caveat : time rank calculation for multiple time-varying variables (i.e. multichannel sequences in a tidy long-format tibble)

  • Dataset is recorded in discrete time, with one value per individual per month.
    The RSA receipt variable is genuinely discrete, since RSA is calculated for full months.

  • When working with one row per individual per month, we need to be careful about missing months in a sequence: the previous or next row does not necessarily correspond to the previous or next calendar month. Missing data for an individual-month may appear either as a missing row or as an NA value in the row for that month.

  • Sometimes, however, I need to work with continuous-time variables.
    For example, when analysing the trajectories of children receiving child welfare intervention, the interventions may begin and end on specific dates and overlap.

In such cases, I often discretise the data.

  • When working with multiple time-varying variables , row numbers ordered by ID and date may not represent the correct time ranks. Use dplyr::min_rank, dplyr::dense_rank() or calculate the time difference from the start date.

From TraMineR to the tidyverse ?

  • Observation: For basic longitudinal statistics, I use TraMineR less and less, in favour of tidyverse packages and data.table (via dtplyr).

  • Why? TraMineR works with objects of class “stslist”. This requires creating another large object in the environment. The format is fairly rigid and does not readily support basic statistical analyses.

  • In detail:

    • Increasing size of my datasets

    • Simplification of the statistical analyses carried out to meet professionals’ needs

    • I’ve been shaped by the tidyverse way of thinking about data management and workflow design. So I need ggplot2 and compatibles datas inputs

    • It can be difficult to obtain clean trajectory data :

      • for RSA datas it’s OK (a single qualitative variable observed over time)

      • But others themes (child protection, autonomy policies) are more complexes : multidimensional longitudinal data and simultaneous events. Long “tidy” datasets are very convenient for these purposes.

  • I keep using TraMineR mainly for :

    • seqdist() : a very complete and very well documented function for optimal matching of sequences.

    • seqefsub() : usefull for complex subsequences with numerous events.

  • Observation: I use TraMineR less and less, in favour of tidyverse packages and data.table (mainly via dtplyr).

  • Why? I’m not entirely sure, but I think the following factors play a role:

    • The increasing size of my datasets

    • Simplification of the statistical analyses carried out to meet professionals’ needs

    • I’ve been shaped by the tidyverse way of thinking about data management and workflow design

    • Then, I need ggplot2 (and compatible datas inputs) for my visualisations

    • It can be difficult to obtain clean trajectory data :

      • for RSA data it’s OK (a single qualitative variable observed over time)

      • others topics (child protection, autonomy policies) are more complex : multidimensional longitudinal data and simultaneous events. Tidyverse very convenient for this uses.

  • I keep using TraMineR mainly for seqdist() when needed : a very complete and very well documented function.

The {ViCaTraj} package

https://github.com/ECLOH/ViCaTraj/tree/ViCaTraj-2.0

  • A package built with no code-sharing purpose, used only by me (so far, at least).

  • A package with a history:

    • Initially, a modularised Shiny app (ViCaTraj::ViCaTraj(), developed with some input from Conseil Dép. de Loire-Atlantique), designed to let users with no R experience :
      • access a database
      • apply complex filters to data over time
      • conduct longitudinal analyses, mainly using TraMineR functions for visualisation, longitudinal statistics, and optimal sequence matching.
    • Now, a collection of R functions for longitudinal analysis, designed to fit naturally into tidyverse workflows and work seamlessly with tidy data.

The application has been used outside the Isère Departement, mainly in the “Cahiers territoriaux” de la “Cour des Comptes” concerning RSA benefits on several départements, for performing optimal-matching-based clustering of sequences, and ploting alluvial plots.

  • The situation back in 2019:

    • 4 GB of RAM
    • I mainly knew base R

  • So:

    • I didn’t have the resources to read and analyse the large XML source files. I loaded everything and put it all into a data frame, which led to errors and misunderstandings about the file structure.
    • I managed the database using one data frame per month, stored in a list and saved with save(). Whenever I added a new month, I had to load everything and save the whole list again.
    • Cleaning the database to make it GDPR-compliant was almost impossible. I had to load all the data frames and search and filter through the list. If something went wrong, it was very hard to debug.

2. The {ViCaTraj} workflow: database management and data formatting

func_XML_TO_PARQUET() : load monthly .xml and increment .parquet

This core function loads monthly XML files and append them to the parquet database.

  • Step 1 : XML
    • xml2::load_xml()
    • xml2::xml_remove() : select nodes
    • xml2::as_list() : very slow, but necessary ?
      • convenient and create a readable R object in session
      • very, very, very slow. Between 10-15 minutes per month (≃ 50K households). I tried other tools but the time saving is not very important and I lose code clarity.
        I’d be interested to hear your ideas! 😊

  • Step 2 : create individuals df from list

    • ViCaTraj::func_rename_node_personne(): deal with duplicated nodes names (multiples persons by household node), find persons roles in households

    • ViCaTraj::func_format_ListToDf(): create one data.frame by list element

  • Step 3: bind, clean and save
    • bind and clean
    • create and recode variables
    • arrow::write_dataset() on the grouped data.frame (by date)
  • Next, connect to the database : bd <- arrow::open_dataset(".../my_database_folder")

func_Find_OldID() : making data GDPR compliant

First cleaning of the datas : each month remove old IDs folowing DPRG rules

→ Data relating to all individuals who left “definitively” the RSA six years ago must be deleted.

With few RAM and no other methods than charging all database in R sessions then saving for deleting, this operations was tedious.

Now is simple and fast, as the dataset is never loaded in R sessions thanks to arrow:

  1. In the opened database, find IDs with no RSA for a choosen number of years:

    df_ID_delete <- bd |> 
   select(ID_hh, RSA_simple, DATE) |>  
  filter(
    RSA_simple == "RSA" |
      RSA_simple == "SUSPENDU" ) |> 
  ViCaTraj::func_Find_OldID(nb_keep = 6) |> collect()

  2. Remove the IDs from the database in session:

    bdd_clean <- bd |> 
  anti_join( df_ID_delete |>  select(-DATE), 
  by = "ID_hh")

  1. Keep only DATE with modifications (to simplify the final save operation):

    bdd_clean_tosave <- bdd_clean |> 
 semi_join(
   df_ID_delete |> 
     select(DATE), 
   by = "DATE")

  2. saving the updated and filtered database and so erase IDs:

     arrow::write_dataset(
         existing_data_behavior = "delete_matching", 
         dataset = (bdd_clean_tosave|> group_by(DATE, INSTITUTION)), 
         path = "/database_location")

func_recode_event(): preparing data for trajectory & survival analysis

For survival analysis or a simple distribution analysis, I need to :

  • Distinguish Exits from censoring.
  • Distinguish between permanent and temporary exits (like “gaps” or “right” parmaters in TraMineR::seqdef()).
data_long_rcd <- data_long_corr |>
  ViCaTraj::func_recode_event(
    time_col = date, 
# Time column: Date or numeric
    indiv_col = ID_hh, 
    start_col = START, 
# Start time for each individual
# (NULL: date of first non-NA value by ID)
    end_col = NULL, 
# End time for each individual
# (NULL: date of last non-NA value by ID)
    event_col = RSA_simple_corr, 
# Variable of interest
    start_time = NULL, 
# Follow-up start time
# (NULL: uses the beginning of the data)
    censor_time = NULL, 
# Censoring time
# (NULL: uses the time step after the last month in the data)
    clean_na = FALSE 
# Do not replace missing values with defaults
  )

For survival analysis or a simple distribution analysis, I need to describe exits :

  • Exiting is the main event of interest and must be distinguished from censoring.
  • Distinguishing between permanent and temporary exits could be useful for those responsible for managing and overseeing the scheme.

3. The {ViCaTraj} workflow: use the data

Using standard {dplyr} syntax for basic statistics

  • TraMineR provides a nice function to have states distribution along time : TraMineR::seqstatd(), with grouping options. But the result is in an inconvenient format, and the input has to be a specific stslist object.

  • With tidyverse and a tidy dataset, it’s quite simple.
    Bonus : it handles multiple states easily by “ID - date” couples.

Code 
stat_dist_time <- data_long_rcd |>
    filter(START == as.Date("2023-01-01")) |> 
    group_by(date, RCD_STATE) |> 
    summarise(Ni = n_distinct(ID_hh)) |>
    group_by(date) |> 
    mutate(prop = Ni / sum(Ni))
RSA receipt among households newly entering the scheme in January 2023
date RCD_STATE Ni prop
2023-01-01 RSA 1268 100%
2023-02-01 RSA 1268 100%
2023-03-01 RSA 1172 92.4%
2023-03-01 exit 68 5.4%
2023-03-01 temporary exit 28 2.2%
2023-04-01 RSA 996 78.5%
2023-04-01 exit 175 13.8%
2023-04-01 temporary exit 97 7.6%

Other basic statistics using tidy, long-format data:

  • Time spent in each state: Count the rows or distinct dates for each ID–state pair.
  • Average time spent in each state: Calculate the mean time spent in each state.
  • Sequence length: Count the distinct dates, or calculate the difference between the minimum and maximum dates.
  • Frequent sequences: Use pivot_wider(), then group_by() across all variables and count the rows.
  • …

Using standard {dplyr} syntax for basic statistics : plot

RSA receipt for new entrants

ViCaTraj::func_txtran()

Fast and clear equivalent to TraMineR::seqtrate() :

txtran <- data_long_rcd |>  
    dtplyr::lazy_dt() |> 
    filter(RCD_STATE != "censoring") |> 
    #mutate(rank_global = dense_rank(date)) |> 
    ViCaTraj::func_txtran(
      ID = ID_hh, 
      var = RCD_STATE, 
      #full_rank = rank_global, 
      full_rank = NULL,
      date = date, 
      time_step = 1, 
      time_varying = F) |> 
    as_tibble()
⚠️ full_rank is not the same as individual ranks.

    It must be calculated from the complete set of possible time points, including those missing from the dataset.

    See ``ViCaTraj::func_delete_modgap()`` and ``ViCaTraj::func_expand()``.
⚠️ ``date`` has been supplied: calculating global ranks: 

       `data |> ungroup() |> dplyr::dense_rank({{date}})`

ViCaTraj::order_xy_traj(): “index plots” with basic ggplot2 syntax

Inside a “family” of 2 functions : order_xx_...() that complement the forcats::fct_reorder() function for longitudinal data in tidy, long format.

data |>
  mutate(ID_hh = factor(
    ID_hh,
    levels = ViCaTraj::order_xy_traj(VAR = ID_hh, VAR_arrange = RCD_STATE, VAR_ctrl = date, start = "beg"), 
    ordered = TRUE
    )
   )

Conclusion

Conclusion

  • In local government, the demand for longitudinal data is strong but often quite basic: professionals and managers need simple indicators to understand beneficiaries’ pathways and inform their decisions.

  • Yet producing these indicators relies on quit complex data and processing (administrative sources must be cleaned, structured and carefully interpreted over time).

  • {ViCaTraj} provides a simple and practical workflow for creating and using longitudinal database and supporting analyses of entries, exits, returns and trajectories.

  • With well-structured data, many longitudinal analyses can be carried out simply and seamlessly.
    Looking ahead, trajectory analysis could be more naturally conducted using tidy, long-format data.
    Could {ViCaTraj} be a first step in that direction?
